name: Folk
def: Acoustic song rooted in traditional and topical material — voice, guitar and storytelling foregrounded over production.
why: Stripped acoustic backing keeps the focus on lyric, melody and storytelling tradition.
tempoNote: Wide range — tempo follows the song, not the genre.

name: Country
def: White Southern roots music of fiddle, steel guitar and plain-spoken song — descended from folk balladry and the blues.

traits.v: Pedal steel, fiddle, acoustic and electric guitar.

why: Steel guitar and fiddle over simple chords frame a plain, narrative vocal rooted in folk and blues.

name: Cosmic American Music
def: Gram Parsons' name for his fusion of country, soul, R&B and rock — honky-tonk and pedal steel played by long-haired rock musicians for a counterculture audience.

traits.v: Pedal steel, fiddle and Telecaster twang with a rock rhythm section.
Late-60s Los Angeles, between the Sunset Strip and Bakersfield.

why: It brought straight country songcraft into the rock counterculture at a time when the two scenes kept apart.

tracks.why: Parsons' ballad on Sweetheart of the Rodeo, the record that turned a rock band toward Nashville.

name: Americana
def: A modern blend of folk, country, blues and rock — roots instrumentation and songwriting filtered through indie sensibility.

traits.v: Roots palette — acoustic, steel, organ — with a rock band.

why: It recombines folk, country and blues roots within a rock and indie framework, foregrounding songcraft and warmth.

name: Old-Time / Hillbilly
def: Rural Southern white string-band music of fiddle and banjo — Appalachian ballads and dance tunes that seeded country, bluegrass and the folk revival.
why: The fiddle-and-banjo string-band tradition is the Anglo-American root that country and bluegrass grow directly out of.

name: Bluegrass
def: A fast, virtuosic acoustic string music codified by Bill Monroe — breakneck breakdowns, high-lonesome harmony and hot instrumental solos.

traits.v: Virtuosic banjo, fiddle and mandolin solos.

why: It accelerates old-time string-band music into a virtuosic, solo-trading form, with high-lonesome harmony as its signature.

name: Cosmic Country
def: A psychedelic, genre-blurring update of country and Americana — pedal steel and traditional song filtered through synths, soul and an outsider, cosmic sensibility.

traits.v: Pedal steel and twang beside synths and strings.

why: It reimagines country and Americana through psychedelic production and soul, blurring roots tradition with modern pop.

tracks.why: Its psychedelic strings under classic country songwriting defined the cosmic turn.

tempoNote: Variable across its country, soul and psych sources.

name: Country Rock
def: Rock bands playing country — pedal steel, Telecaster twang and close harmony over a rock rhythm section, from the Byrds' Nashville turn in 1968 to the Eagles' radio dominance in the early 70s.

traits.v: Pedal steel, banjo and Telecaster beside a rock bass-and-drums backbeat.
Stacked three- and four-part country-style harmony on the chorus.
Relaxed mid-tempo shuffle or straight 4/4 — never honky-tonk fast.
Los Angeles 1968–74: the Troubadour, Laurel Canyon and the Asylum Records roster.

why: It keeps country's instruments and harmony singing but plays them with a rock band's volume and a counterculture audience in mind, so the twang reads as warmth rather than tradition.

tracks.why: Banjo, Telecaster and stacked harmony on a 1972 top-20 single — country rock reaching the mainstream it was built for.

tempoNote: Mid-tempo shuffles and easy 4/4 — the lope of 'Take It Easy' rather than honky-tonk drive.

name: Singer-Songwriter
def: The solo writer-performer as the whole point — confessional first-person lyrics, acoustic guitar or piano up front, and restrained studio backing that stays out of the voice's way.

traits.v: Intimate, conversational, close-miked; the words carry the performance.
Open tunings, suspended chords and jazz-tinged piano voicings beneath simple melodies.
Dry, warm and uncluttered — acoustic instrument, voice and a light rhythm section.
Laurel Canyon and the Troubadour, 1968–72 — Joni Mitchell, James Taylor, Carole King and Jackson Browne writing within walking distance of each other.

why: Folk's lyric-first plainness is turned inward: private experience replaces topical protest, and the arrangement is built to frame one voice telling the truth.

tracks.why: Confessional lyric, fingerpicked acoustic and a discreet rhythm section — the 1970 record that put the format on the radio.

tempoNote: Ballad to easy mid-tempo; rubato and conversational phrasing are common.
